title: The Fifth Era of Science: Artificial Scientific Intelligence
gist: Nina Miolane (byline in text; republished from PLOS Biology) argues science is entering a fifth era of 'artificial scientific intelligence' after empirical, theoretical, computational and data-driven eras, with Google, Lila Sciences and Sakana building AI scientists. Autonomy works in data-rich chemistry and materials science, but in biomedical imaging and cryo-EM, small (~1000x too few images) and noisy data mean human experts must steer AI and curate data.

insights.claim: Science has progressed through four technology-defined eras — empirical, theoretical, computational (from the 1950s) and data-driven (21st-century machine learning) — and is now entering a fifth era of artificial scientific intelligence.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Frames AI-for-science as a paradigm shift in how discovery is produced, not an incremental tool upgrade.
insights.quote: Today, we stand at the doorstep of the fifth era of science — the artificial scientific intelligence era

insights.claim: In 2024 AI helped win a Nobel Prize for the first time, when DeepMind's AlphaFold solved protein-structure prediction, a decades-old problem crucial for medicine and drug discovery.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: AlphaFold is the proof point legitimizing AI-driven discovery investment in drug discovery.
insights.quote: In 02024, artificial intelligence (AI), for the first time, helped win a Nobel Prize.

insights.claim: AlphaFold's success was a data-driven-era achievement made possible by learning from the Protein Data Bank, a large structured public dataset.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Large curated public datasets are the precondition for AI breakthroughs; watch which fields have their equivalent.

insights.claim: Companies including Google, Lila Sciences and Sakana are unveiling 'AI scientists' that go beyond assisting research to generating hypotheses, testing them and driving discoveries on their own.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Names the commercial players racing for autonomous-science platforms — a nascent category to track.
insights.quote: companies like Google, Lila Sciences, and Sakana are unveiling AI scientists that not only assist research but drive discoveries
insights.locator: Today, we stand at the doorstep

themes.theme: Where autonomous AI science works today

insights.claim: Autonomous AI exploration works best in fields where experimental feedback is tractable, simulations are mature and data is plentiful and structured — such as chemistry and materials science.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: A screening heuristic for which AI-for-science verticals can scale autonomy first.
insights.quote: These are domains where experimental feedback is relatively tractable, simulations are mature and the data is plentiful and structured.
insights.locator: In some fields, perhaps we can.

insights.claim: In chemistry, organic synthesis of complex drug-like molecules is now guided by interpretable AI models that help scientists plan each step.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: AI retrosynthesis planning is already operational and relevant to pharma R&D productivity.
insights.locator: In some fields, perhaps we can.

insights.claim: In materials science, generative AI can design novel inorganic compounds with tailored mechanical, electronic and magnetic properties with minimal human tuning.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Generative materials design could compress discovery cycles for batteries, semiconductors and magnets.
insights.quote: generative AI can design novel inorganic compounds with tailored mechanical, electronic, and magnetic properties
insights.locator: In some fields, perhaps we can.

themes.theme: Data scarcity bottleneck in biomedical imaging

insights.claim: In many scientific fields, letting AI run autonomously today is premature because specialized scientific data differ sharply from what large vision models are trained on — biomedical imaging being the clearest case.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Pushes back on 'AI scientist' hype; autonomy claims in biomedicine deserve skepticism.
insights.quote: letting an AI run the show today would be like sending a self-driving car down a dirt road with half a map and no GPS

insights.claim: Biomedical imaging datasets are tiny by AI standards because collection needs specialized equipment and professionals, labeling requires expert time, and privacy regulations limit access.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Data acquisition, labeling and privacy access are the moat — value accrues to whoever owns curated medical data.

insights.claim: MedPix, a leading medical imaging database, holds only about 59,000 images and the Allen Cell Feature Explorer about 32,000 3D stem-cell images — roughly a thousand times fewer than AI typically needs to perform.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Quantifies a ~1000x data gap in medical AI; data-generation businesses address a real bottleneck.
insights.quote: That is about a thousand times fewer than what is needed for AI to perform.

insights.claim: Mathematically redesigned neural network building blocks can stay robust on small data, working even with a single layer and two convolutional filters where traditional models collapse.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Small-data, structure-aware architectures are an alternative path to scale-heavy models in science.
insights.quote: even with just a single layer and two convolutional filters
insights.locator: Scientists are redefining AI to do

insights.claim: Scientists also reshape the data ecosystem — choosing what to collect and stitching together fragmented specialized datasets — to train models for tasks such as brain tumor classification and diabetic retinopathy grading.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Dataset aggregation/curation is itself a value-creating layer in medical AI.
insights.locator: Scientists are redefining AI to do

insights.claim: Cryo-electron microscopy images are so noisy that important details are about 100 times weaker than the noise, in stark contrast to the crisp images mainstream AI vision models are trained on.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Off-the-shelf vision foundation models will underperform on scientific instruments without domain adaptation.
insights.quote: the important details are 100 times weaker than the noise
insights.locator: But scientific data is not just scarce

insights.claim: A cryo-EM breakthrough paired a denoising module with a foundation model, but only worked because experts cleaned, annotated and aggregated 529 verified cryo-EM datasets into one training set.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Expert data curation, not model scale alone, unlocked the result — human-curated data remains the binding constraint.
insights.quote: aggregating 529 verified cryo-EM datasets into one large training set that AI could learn from
insights.locator: Yet scientists have techniques to extract

insights.claim: The fifth era of science will not sideline human scientists; breakthroughs will come from human expertise guiding AI and AI augmenting human expertise.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Expect value in human-in-the-loop scientific platforms rather than fully autonomous labs, at least outside data-rich fields.
insights.quote: the fifth era of artificial scientific intelligence is not void of human scientists: quite the opposite

insights.claim: AI in science is like a superhuman, sleepless intern: enormous potential, but without guidance grounded in scientific knowledge it is more likely to 'set the lab on fire' than advance science.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Unsupervised AI-science outputs carry error risk; validation and oversight are critical.
insights.quote: they are more likely to set the lab on fire than to push science forward

insights.claim: The labs that thrive will be those where domain experts and AI specialists work in sync or where scientists master both, requiring interdisciplinary university programs.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Hybrid domain+AI talent is scarce and will command a premium; watch interdisciplinary training pipelines.
insights.quote: The labs that thrive will be those where domain experts and AI specialists work in sync or where scientists master both.
